clue.text: Humorist featured in Arthur Bergson's work

indicators.note: featured in says the answer appears inside the run of the clue words that follow

explanation.surface: A comic writer turns up in the work of the French philosopher Henri Bergson, who wrote on laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featured in' tells you to look inside 'Arthur Bergson's'; James Thurber was an American humorist and cartoonist.
explanation.definitionFit: James Thurber was a celebrated American comic writer and cartoonist for The New Yorker.

clue.text: "Henry and ,/ And Miguel of Spain, stood with Shakespeare at the top…" (Kipling)

definitions.text: "Henry and ,/ And Miguel of Spain, stood with Shakespeare at the top…" (Kipling)

parts.words: "Henry and ,/ And Miguel of Spain, stood with Shakespeare at the top…" (Kipling)
parts.note: a quotation from Kipling's poem The Craftsman-related verses with one name left out; Henry is Fielding and Miguel is Cervantes, and the gap is Smollett's first name

explanation.surface: Kipling lines naming great novelists who stand beside Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobias Smollett, the eighteenth-century novelist, fills the gap between Henry Fielding and Miguel de Cervantes in Kipling's list.

clue.text: Defiled part of prince's "monstrous carbuncle" -an eyesore meriting it

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a portion of the letters in the words that follow

explanation.surface: Prince Charles's famous jibe at a modern building plan as an ugly blot that earned the insult.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' points into 'carbuncle" -an'. In 1984 Prince Charles called a proposed National Gallery extension in London 'a monstrous carbuncle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something defiled is soiled, impure or polluted.

clue.text: Founder of influential magazine: Ebony, possibly?

explanation.surface: Asking whether the founder of a major magazine might be Ebony, the American monthly.
explanation.definitionFit: William Blackwood founded Blackwood's Magazine in Edinburgh; ebony is a dark timber, a black kind of tree material.

clue.text: Absurdly vain monarch was piano virtuoso

indicators.note: absurdly means in a ridiculous way, telling us the letters of the next words are scrambled

explanation.surface: A ridiculously conceited king turns out to have been a great pianist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absurdly' rearranges VAINMONARCH; 'was' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Sergei Rachmaninov was a Russian composer and one of the greatest concert pianists of his day.

clue.text: American sage in A Room With a View

definitions.text: in A Room With a View

explanation.surface: An American thinker appears in E. M. Forster's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson was the American transcendentalist sage; Mr Emerson and his son George are characters in Forster's A Room With a View.

clue.text: James Agate offered nothing in support of example

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece in support of another sits under it, so the zero comes below the abbreviation

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation for 'for example'
O, the figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: A critic gave nothing to back up a sample.
explanation.walkthrough: James Agate, the British drama critic, published his diaries in nine volumes under this title.
explanation.definitionFit: James Agate's diaries appeared as a series of volumes titled with the Latin word for the self.

clue.text: Miss Landon's novel sort of Churchill

definitions.text: Miss Landon's novel sort of Churchill

parts.words: Miss Landon's novel sort of Churchill
parts.note: The clue asks which kind of Churchill, i.e. the first name in that title

explanation.surface: A Victorian woman writer's novel about a certain Churchill.
explanation.definitionFit: Letitia Elizabeth Landon's 1837 novel is titled with a woman's first name followed by Churchill.

clue.text: Conrad Potter Aiken's fighting man takes money with hesitation

parts.note: soldi are Italian coins, plural of soldo, so a word for money
er is the sound of a speaker hesitating

explanation.surface: A warrior in an American poet's work accepts cash with some reluctance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' and 'with' are link words. Aiken published The Soldier: A Poem in 1944.
explanation.definitionFit: Aiken's 1944 poem is about a fighting man, and the word means a serving member of an army.

clue.text: What Leacock's novels were

parts.note: seems a disparaging verdict on the Canadian humorist Stephen Leacock

explanation.surface: A critic's damning judgment on Stephen Leacock's fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Leacock's 1911 parody collection is titled Nonsense Novels, so absurd rubbish is literally what they were.

clue.text: Taleteller with a big mouth in Italy

definitions.text: with a big mouth in Italy

explanation.surface: A storyteller is described as a loudmouth in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Italian bocca is a mouth and -accio a suffix meaning big or ugly, so the name reads as 'big mouth'.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the Decameron, a hundred stories; his surname splits into Italian for a coarse, oversized mouth.

clue.text: King's lady greatly taken with Paris

definitions.text: King's lady greatly taken with Paris

parts.words: King's lady greatly taken with Paris
parts.note: reads like a royal consort enjoying the French capital, but means the Greek queen of Sparta carried off by the Trojan prince Paris

explanation.surface: A queen falls in love with the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Menelaus's wife in Greek myth was abducted by (and infatuated with) the Trojan prince Paris, starting the Trojan War.

clue.text: "What! Keep away?" (Othello)

parts.note: a quotation from Othello with two words left out; the full line is Bianca's 'What! keep ... away? seven days and nights?', and the missing words are the answer

explanation.surface: A line of Othello asking why someone stays away.
explanation.definitionFit: Bianca reproaches Cassio in Othello for staying away seven days, i.e. a span of time, and the gap in the quotation is filled by that phrase.

clue.text: Place in Paris recalled by Proust

explanation.surface: A Parisian spot comes back to the memory of the novelist Proust.
explanation.definitionFit: La Madeleine is a famous church and square in Paris; in Proust's novel a small sponge cake dipped in tea triggers involuntary memory.

clue.text: Vulnerable, like Nabokov's oeuvre, without his 1964 output

parts.note: The Defence, Nabokov's chess novel, appeared in English in 1964
less means without, as in 'penniless'

explanation.surface: Nabokov's whole body of work, minus one year's book, is exposed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like Nabokov's oeuvre' frames the joke: his work without The Defence would be the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being vulnerable means being open to attack, with no protection.

clue.text: Where the chief interest of Rubens lay, roughly speaking

definitions.text: Where the chief interest of Rubens lay

explanation.surface: An art historian says the painter Rubens cared most about something, as an approximation.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubens famously painted plump, curvaceous bodies; the idiom also means approximately, giving numbers rounded off.

clue.text: Illume gig in order to see opera composer

indicators.note: putting letters in order means arranging them properly, so the jumbled letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Lighting up a show so that you can see someone who writes operas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in order' rearranges ILLUMEGIG; Pietro Alessandro Guglielmi was an 18th-century Italian opera composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pietro Alessandro Guglielmi wrote around a hundred operas in eighteenth-century Italy.

clue.text: The gentleman was not for burning

definitions.text: The gentleman was not for burning

parts.words: The gentleman was not for burning
parts.note: echoes Christopher Fry's play The Lady's Not for Burning, but refers to the man in the Book of Daniel who came out of Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace unharmed

explanation.surface: A male twist on the title of Christopher Fry's verse comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Daniel this companion of Shadrach and Meshach survived the furnace without being burnt.

clue.text: Swift definition of outsize

parts.note: Swift looks like 'quick', but it is Jonathan Swift, whose land of giants in Gulliver's Travels gives the adjective for enormous

explanation.surface: A quick dictionary entry for the word for very large.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from the land of giants in Gulliver's Travels and means gigantic.

clue.text: Circle agents change for scene of performance

definitions.note: a noun phrase for a place; the answer is a phrase meaning at that place

parts.note: a circle is round like the letter O

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters in the following word

explanation.surface: Theatre agents swap seats in the dress circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circle' looks like the theatre's dress circle, but it supplies only a ring-shaped letter; 'change' scrambles the agents, and 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the boards of the theatre means being where the performance takes place.

clue.text: Dramatist who had his birthday

parts.note: sounds like a playwright celebrating another year

explanation.surface: A playwright celebrates turning a year older.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodney Ackland, the English playwright, wrote the play Birthday, so it was his.

clue.text: "A land unknown to prose or rhyme; / Where words ne'er crost the Muse's —s " (Burns)

definitions.text: "A land unknown to prose or rhyme; / Where words ne'er crost the Muse's —s " (Burns)

parts.words: "A land unknown to prose or rhyme; / Where words ne'er crost the Muse's —s " (Burns)
parts.note: Burns lines with one word left out; the dash plus s is a plural noun for the flax-comb, the steel teeth across which words are drawn

explanation.surface: Robert Burns describes a land poetry has never touched.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots a heckle is a comb for dressing flax, and Burns pictures words being combed across the Muse's teeth.

clue.text: Idle revue does poorly

indicators.note: poorly means done badly, telling us the letters of the two words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A stage revue performs badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poorly' rearranges REVUE and DOES into the French loanword meaning unoccupied.
explanation.definitionFit: The French loanword describes someone with nothing to do, unoccupied or at a loose end.

clue.text: Occurrence revealing first lady with book

parts.note: Eve was the first woman in Genesis
NT, the New Testament, is a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A happening reveals a president's wife carrying a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First lady' suggests a president's wife, but here it is the first woman in the Bible; 'revealing' and 'with' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: An occurrence is something that happens, a happening or incident.

clue.text: My wife is learning now Sir, to weave " (Beaumont and Fletcher, The Scornful Lady)

parts.words: My wife is learning now Sir, to weave " (Beaumont and Fletcher, The Scornful Lady)
parts.note: a quotation from the Jacobean comedy The Scornful Lady with its last word left out; the missing word is the thing being woven

explanation.surface: A husband in a Jacobean comedy reports what his wife is learning to weave.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a linen tape or braid, a thing a woman of the period might weave on a small loom.

clue.text: Delete English level

parts.note: to rase (raze) is to level a building to the ground

explanation.surface: An instruction to remove a level of the English course.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete text is to wipe it out or rub it away.

clue.text: Sound mettle of Bhabani Bhattacharya's predator

parts.note: sound mettle is firm resolve, the nerve of something hard and tempered like a strong metal
a hawk is a predatory bird

explanation.surface: Praise for the courage of a bird of prey in an Indian writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: Bhabani Bhattacharya, an Indian novelist, wrote the story collection Steel Hawk and Other Stories, so his name stands for the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel Hawk and Other Stories is a collection by the Indian writer Bhabani Bhattacharya, so it is his work.

clue.text: Hassall's urgent appeal to fortified town?

definitions.text: Hassall's urgent appeal to fortified town?

parts.words: Hassall's urgent appeal to fortified town?
parts.note: Christopher Hassall's 1940 poetry collection was titled .... ... Ludlow, Ludlow being a Shropshire castle town

explanation.surface: A poet sends a desperate call to a walled town.
explanation.definitionFit: The distress signal is an urgent call for help, and it opens Hassall's book title addressed to Ludlow.

clue.text: Matricide concealed in forest, escaping censure

indicators.note: concealed in says the answer is tucked inside the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A mother-killer hides in the woods and avoids blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealed in' points into 'forest escaping'; the surface also fits the myth, as Orestes was acquitted by the Areopagus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Orestes killed his mother Clytemnestra to avenge his father Agamemnon.

clue.text: Lewd sin perhaps worthy of Felix Krull?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters given are only one possible arrangement, so they are to be reshuffled

explanation.surface: Lewd sinning might befit the roguish hero of Thomas Mann's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges LEWDSIN. Felix Krull is the confidence trickster hero of Thomas Mann's Confessions of Felix Krull.
explanation.definitionFit: Felix Krull is a con man, so a fraud or deception is the kind of act worthy of him.
